title: Plaintiffs Push for Fast Ruling in $100,000 H-1B Fee Case as Government Seeks Pause
excerpt: In Global Nurse Force v. Trump, employers and workers want a California court to move to summary judgment on the $100,000 H-1B payment, while the administration asks to freeze the case until the Ninth Circuit rules on its appeal.
body:
• Employers and workers challenging the $100,000 H-1B fee have asked a California federal court to move quickly toward a final ruling, while the Trump administration wants the case paused until the Ninth Circuit decides its appeal.
  • The fight is over scheduling, not the fee itself: Judge Gilliam's September 30 order already blocks the fee policies, and a separate Massachusetts injunction also bars collection.
  • Plaintiffs want the administrative record produced by November 3; the government proposes producing it only 30 days after the appeals court acts. The stay motion is not even argued until January 14, 2027.
  • For Indian professionals and their employers: petitions are currently being processed without the $100,000 payment, but that relief rests on preliminary orders an appeals court could undo.

Employers and workers challenging the Trump administration's $100,000 fee on new H-1B visa petitions have asked a federal court in California to move quickly toward a final ruling, while the government wants the case put on hold until an appeals court rules, according to IANS, reporting on a joint case management statement filed on October 20 in Global Nurse Force v. Trump.

The plaintiffs told the court they "challenge the lawfulness of a $100,000 payment requirement as a condition of processing H-1B visa petitions and entry into the United States." The government countered that pressing ahead now would waste resources while the Ninth Circuit considers its appeal.

Two courts have already blocked the fee

President Donald Trump imposed the fee through Proclamation 10973, signed on September 19, 2025, and extended it with Proclamation 11069 on September 18, 2026. The charge applies to new H-1B petitions and sits on top of the program's existing filing costs, which is why it landed hardest on employers hiring from India, the source of the large majority of H-1B workers.

https://x.com/JohnBasham/status/2115291870536376662

On September 30, Judge Gilliam granted the plaintiffs' motion for a preliminary injunction in part, denied the government's motion to dismiss, and denied class certification without prejudice. The government appealed to the Ninth Circuit Court of Appeals on October 9 and the same day moved to stay the district court proceedings. A separate injunction from a federal court in Massachusetts also blocks the fee nationwide, a point the government itself raised: "The outcome of this case will not change any status quo given the universal injunction entered in the District of Massachusetts," it argued, adding that further litigation "only wastes the Parties' and Court's resources, and might well result in a duplicative appeal."

"Defendants maintain that further motions practice is inappropriate while the Ninth Circuit considers threshold jurisdictional issues."

— US government filing in Global Nurse Force v. Trump

What each side wants next

The plaintiffs proposed that the government produce the administrative record — the internal documents behind the fee — by November 3, the first step toward summary judgment. They also put the government on notice: "Plaintiffs are monitoring Defendants' compliance with this Court's September 30, 2026 order and may seek enforcement of the order if warranted." The government proposed producing the record only 30 days after the appeals court's mandate, or 30 days after any order denying the stay. The stay motion itself is set for a hearing on January 14, 2027, which means the California case is unlikely to reach a final judgment this year.

The filing lists two other pending appeals on the fee: California v. Mullin in the First Circuit and Chamber of Commerce v. DHS in the District of Columbia Circuit, which was argued on March 9, 2026. We mapped that three-circuit split in our earlier coverage of why the $100,000 fee fight is not over. The core legal questions, both sides agreed, are whether the President's proclamation and its extensions are "ultra vires" — beyond his legal authority — and whether the State Department and the Department of Homeland Security violated the Administrative Procedure Act in implementing it. The plaintiffs are represented by groups including the Justice Action Center, Democracy Forward, the South Asian American Justice Collaborative (SAAJCO) and the law firm Cohen Milstein Sellers & Toll, as GreatAndhra also reported.

What this means for H-1B employers and workers

Nothing changes today. Because two injunctions block the fee, employers filing new petitions without the $100,000 payment have been receiving approvals. What the scheduling fight decides is how long that relief lasts. If the California case races to summary judgment, a final ruling against the fee could replace the temporary orders with something harder to dislodge. If the case is paused and an appeals court later revives the fee, employers who built hiring plans around the injunctions would face the charge again with little warning. For Indian professionals in the US hiring pipeline — and the hospitals, tech firms and universities sponsoring them — the practical advice from this filing is narrow: the fee is blocked for now, the block is contested on three appellate fronts, and the next hard date is the January 14, 2027 stay hearing.
